doc.title: Billy Taylor — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: New York scene and bebop community
title: Accompaniment style, the Mad Monk and Monk's 52nd Street Theme
summary: With Eddie South's trio he developed his harmonic accompaniment, mixing Ellington voicings, stride and bop on his piece The Mad Monk.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: the harmony I wanted, anywhere I wanted on the piano. So I really developed the style of accompaniment that I was attracted to and I flushed out some of the harmonic things that I had heard Ellington do, and added to them some things that worked for me. I had started doing this on my first record. I mean I did a piece called the Mad Monk and in the Mad Monk you’ll hear the same thing that Ellington did, the same kind of voicing just in a blues context. I mean I made a little melody out of it. And the Mad Monk that I’m referring to is Thelonious Monk because what this has got is it’s a stride, it’s basically after I do this Ellington type thing, I play some stride and I play the release of the piece. Its got a little pseudo bebop line and so once again, I’m mixing everything I’ve got all in this 32 bar piece [laughter], because in those days I had no reason to believe it wouldn’t work. I mean I’d say well, you know, a dab of this and a dab of that will work. And sometimes it did, and sometimes it did a lot better. For instance, that concept was much better defined by Monk himself when he wrote 52nd Street Theme. He used a riff and then he used a very complicated bebop release, then he went back to the riff, which Dizzy and many other guys had used as a device. I wasn’t that well grounded in the New York style of playing to be able to do that at that point.
